name: The Continuum Hypothesis
statement: There is no size of infinity strictly between the counting numbers and the real number line.
statementAccent: no size of infinity strictly between
meaning: The continuum hypothesis conjectures that there is no set whose size is strictly between that of the integers and that of the real numbers. Cantor showed that infinities come in different sizes: the integers form the smallest infinite set, countable infinity, while the real numbers form a strictly larger infinity, the continuum. The hypothesis asserts that the continuum is the very next size up, with no intermediate infinity in between; in the language of cardinal numbers, two to the power of the countable infinity equals the first uncountable cardinal. Posed by Georg Cantor in the 1870s, it was the first of Hilbert's twenty-three problems, and its eventual resolution is one of the most philosophically startling episodes in the history of mathematics.
mechanism: The astonishing answer is that the continuum hypothesis can neither be proved nor disproved from the standard axioms of set theory, the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms with the axiom of choice; it is independent of them. Kurt Godel showed in 1940 that the hypothesis cannot be disproved, by constructing a model of set theory, the constructible universe, in which it holds. Paul Cohen showed in 1963 that it cannot be proved either, by inventing the method of forcing to build a model in which it fails. Together these results establish that the axioms simply do not decide the question: one can consistently add the continuum hypothesis or its negation, so both the hypothesis and its denial yield coherent set theories.

examples.text: David Hilbert made Cantor's continuum problem the very first of his famous 1900 list of twenty-three problems, marking it as a central challenge for the coming century.
In 1940 Kurt Godel proved the continuum hypothesis consistent with the axioms of set theory, showing it cannot be refuted, using his constructible universe.
In 1963 Paul Cohen proved the hypothesis cannot be derived from the axioms either, inventing forcing, a technique that won him the Fields Medal and reshaped set theory.

variants.name: The generalised continuum hypothesis
variants.text: The stronger claim that for every infinite cardinal there is no size strictly between it and its power set, likewise independent of the standard axioms.

variants.name: New axioms and its truth value
variants.text: Ongoing work seeking additional axioms, such as large-cardinal or forcing axioms, that would settle the hypothesis, with figures like Woodin arguing it is really false.

whyItMatters: The continuum hypothesis is a landmark in the foundations of mathematics because its independence proof showed that a precise, natural question about the infinite can be formally undecidable from the accepted axioms, a concrete realisation of the limits Godel's incompleteness theorems had signalled. Cohen's method of forcing, invented to settle it, became one of the most powerful tools in modern set theory, spawning a vast landscape of independence results. Philosophically, it forces a choice about what mathematical truth means: whether the hypothesis has a definite answer awaiting new axioms, or whether set-theoretic reality genuinely branches, a debate still alive among logicians.

working.text: start from Cantor's result that the reals are strictly larger than the integers, then ask whether anything sits between them in size.
accept that the standard axioms neither prove nor refute the hypothesis, by Godel's 1940 and Cohen's 1963 results, so it is formally undecidable.
to give the question an answer, look to candidate extra axioms; without them the hypothesis has no truth value fixed by the usual set theory.

limits: The hypothesis is not false and not true within the standard axioms; it is independent, so any attempt to settle it from Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with choice alone is doomed. Godel's and Cohen's results are relative consistency proofs assuming set theory itself is consistent, which cannot be proved from within by Godel's second incompleteness theorem. Whether the hypothesis has a real answer depends on one's philosophy of mathematics and on which further axioms, if any, one is willing to adopt, and no such axiom has won general acceptance, so the deeper question of its truth remains open even as its formal independence is settled.
misreadings: Independence does not mean the question is meaningless or that mathematicians simply gave up; it is a proved theorem that the axioms cannot decide it. It does not mean the hypothesis is false, nor that it is true, only that both it and its negation are consistent with the standard axioms. And Cantor's underlying result that the reals outnumber the integers is a proved theorem, not part of what is undecided; what is undecidable is solely whether an intermediate size of infinity can exist, not whether the two infinities differ.
origin: Formulated by Georg Cantor around 1878 as part of his theory of transfinite numbers, made the first of Hilbert's problems in 1900, and shown independent of the standard axioms of set theory by Kurt Godel in 1940 and Paul Cohen in 1963.
